text: In the early 2000s, South Korea“s capital of Seoul was developing at a breathtaking pace, becoming one of Asia”s most prosperous metropolises. From the autumn of 2003 to the summer of 2004, a series of mysterious serial killings erupted in neighborhoods long considered completely safe. Cold, calculated nocturnal break-ins that left no fingerprints baffled police investigators and threw the entire department into disarray. Across South Korea, people were gripped with horror as they realized a cold-blooded predator was stalking the capital in total anonymity. This was the inception of the dark dossier known as Yoo Young-chul — the killer later infamously dubbed The Raincoat Killer.

An elderly wealthy couple was secretly murdered inside their heavily fortified two-story luxury residence. Only weeks later, killings bearing the exact same modus operandi struck other upscale neighborhoods in Gugi-dong and Samsung-dong. What puzzled and disoriented investigators most was that the killer never touched stacks of cash or valuable jewelry sitting in plain sight. He infiltrated through windows or balconies, swung a customized four-kilogram sledgehammer, and targeted solely the elderly or sleeping housekeepers. The perpetrator's objective clearly was not conventional material theft like that of an ordinary burglar. His actions radiated a rabid class hatred and a blind urge to vent his venomous spite against prosperous households.
